analysis.one_liner: Extends full business equipment deductions for a year, paid for by ending an oil company tax break.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let businesses deduct the full cost of new equipment in 2012 instead of spreading it over years, and would let large corporations speed up use of certain tax credits. To keep the bill from adding to the deficit, it would take away a tax deduction that the biggest integrated oil companies claim on their domestic oil and gas production. It was introduced by the top Democrat on the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations planning to buy buildings, machinery, or aircraft in 2012, especially capital-intensive manufacturers, would get an immediate tax deduction for the full purchase price. Large corporations carrying alternative minimum tax credits could convert them into a current cash benefit. The Treasury would gain revenue from taking the domestic production deduction away from major integrated oil companies.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the 100% bonus depreciation allowance through the end of 2012, so businesses can deduct the entire cost of qualifying new assets in the year they are placed in service instead of over the asset's normal life.
Expands the election that lets corporations accelerate their alternative minimum tax credits in lieu of claiming bonus depreciation, effectively letting them cash in those credits sooner.

Denies major integrated oil companies the section 199 deduction for income from domestic production, transportation, or distribution of oil and natural gas, raising revenue that offsets the cost of the depreciation extension.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies would lose a deduction they currently claim on domestic oil and gas income, raising their taxes. To the extent the depreciation extension is not fully offset, taxpayers generally would absorb the cost.

drawbacks.text: The main tax benefits go to corporations, not households: bonus depreciation and AMT credit acceleration are business tax breaks, so any benefit to workers comes only indirectly, through whatever additional investment and hiring the deduction prompts.

Accelerated depreciation mostly shifts deductions earlier in time rather than permanently reducing what companies pay on an asset, so its effect on actual investment decisions is debated and its revenue cost is real in the years it applies.
Narrowing the repeal of the domestic production deduction to major integrated oil companies only spares smaller independent producers, so the pay-for reaches only part of the oil and gas industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is roughly revenue-neutral by design: a broad business tax break for 2012 is paid for by a narrower tax increase on the largest oil companies. Ordinary people would see no direct benefit; the case for the bill rests on the argument that immediate expensing encourages investment and hiring, which is indirect and uncertain. Its clearest concrete effect would have been to take a subsidy away from big oil.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 20, 2012, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major integrated oil companies kept their domestic production tax deduction, since the bill that would have repealed it never advanced. Corporations did not get this particular one-year extension from this bill.

for.name: Sander Levin
for.role: Ranking Member, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 14 Ways and Means Democrats as original cosponsors.

for.name: President Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed to end tax preferences for oil and gas companies, including the domestic production deduction, in his budget proposals during this period.

against.name: Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or committee vote; it sat without action until the Congress ended.

against.name: Major integrated oil companies
against.role: Companies such as ExxonMobil, Chevron, and Shell subject to the repeal provision
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals in this period to strip the domestic production deduction from oil and gas income, arguing it would raise their costs and discourage domestic production.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat (17 of 17) and the bill never reached a vote, so the only recorded positions are partisan; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would strip their domestic production deduction under section 199, raising their taxes by billions over time; keeping the deduction costs the Treasury revenue. Their interest in preserving the break runs against the bill.

industries.industry: Capital-intensive manufacturers and other equipment buyers
industries.note: They would immediately deduct the full cost of new equipment in 2012, a large cash-flow tax benefit. Workers benefit only indirectly if the deduction leads to investment and hiring, and the bill pays for the break with the oil provision.
The bill expands their ability to accelerate minimum tax credits in lieu of bonus depreciation, converting a credit they might otherwise use slowly into faster cash.
